compact_payload.source_guideline: Salvage Therapy for Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO/SUO Guideline
compact_payload.question: A 67-year-old man after prostatectomy has his first-ever detectable ultrasensitive PSA at 0.16 ng/mL after previously undetectable values. No repeat PSA has confirmed a trend. What is the next best step before salvage treatment decisions?
compact_payload.option_a: Repeat PSA to confirm a rising trend
compact_payload.explanation: Option A is correct. A single detectable PSA after prostatectomy should be confirmed with repeat testing before committing the patient to salvage imaging or treatment, because biochemical recurrence is a longitudinal diagnosis. Option B is incorrect because lifelong ADT is not triggered by one low detectable value. Option C is incorrect because cystoscopy does not evaluate prostate bed or nodal recurrence. Option D is incorrect because symptomatic delay can miss a salvage window. Option E is incorrect because intravesical therapy treats bladder cancer, not post-prostatectomy PSA recurrence. Teaching point: Post-prostatectomy recurrence workup starts by confirming the PSA signal, then risk-stratifying the timing and intensity of salvage therapy. Source: American Urological Association. Salvage Therapy for Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO/SUO Guideline.

compact_payload.source_guideline: Salvage Therapy for Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO/SUO Guideline
compact_payload.question: A 70-year-old man with prior prostatectomy has confirmed biochemical recurrence. PSA is 0.32 ng/mL and rising, conventional imaging is negative, and salvage radiation is being considered. What counseling is most appropriate?
compact_payload.option_a: Delay radiation until PSA exceeds 2.0 ng/mL
compact_payload.option_b: Offer salvage radiation while PSA is still low
compact_payload.option_e: Treat if bone scan becomes positive
compact_payload.explanation: Option B is correct. Salvage radiation for post-prostatectomy biochemical recurrence is more effective when delivered at lower PSA levels, so a negative conventional imaging study should not force delay until macroscopic disease appears. Option A is incorrect because waiting for a high PSA reduces the chance of cure. Option C is incorrect because intravesical chemotherapy is unrelated to prostate bed recurrence. Option D is incorrect because the prostate has already been removed. Option E is incorrect because salvage radiation is not reserved for bone-scan-positive disease. Teaching point: The salvage window is PSA-sensitive; negative imaging does not mean there is no potentially curable microscopic recurrence. Source: American Urological Association. Salvage Therapy for Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO/SUO Guideline.

compact_payload.source_guideline: Diagnosis and Treatment of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: AUA/SUO Guideline
compact_payload.question: A 74-year-old man treated for high-risk NMIBC has negative cystoscopy and cytology at follow-up. He asks whether upper-tract surveillance is ever appropriate despite a normal bladder exam. What is guideline-concordant?
compact_payload.option_a: Avoid upper-tract imaging after any negative cystoscopy
compact_payload.option_b: Use bone scan as the upper-tract study
compact_payload.option_c: Consider upper-tract imaging at 1- to 2-year intervals
compact_payload.explanation: Option C is correct. In intermediate- or high-risk NMIBC, surveillance may include upper-tract imaging at 1- to 2-year intervals, even when bladder surveillance is otherwise negative. Option A is incorrect because high-risk urothelial cancer carries upper-tract recurrence risk. Option B is incorrect because bone scan does not evaluate the collecting systems. Option D is incorrect because dipstick testing cannot replace cystoscopic surveillance. Option E is incorrect because nephrectomy is not a surveillance maneuver. Teaching point: Upper-tract surveillance is risk-adapted in NMIBC; low-risk disease avoids routine imaging, while higher-risk disease can justify periodic imaging. Source: American Urological Association. Diagnosis and Treatment of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: AUA/SUO Guideline.

compact_payload.source_guideline: Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline
compact_payload.question: A 55-year-old man with recurrent calcium stones and persistent hypercalciuria starts chlorthalidone. Follow-up urine shows improved calcium but new hypocitraturia and borderline low potassium. What adjunct best fits prevention goals?
compact_payload.explanation: Option D is correct. Potassium citrate can support citrate repletion and potassium balance in a thiazide-treated recurrent calcium stone former, reducing calcium stone risk when hypocitraturia emerges. Option A is incorrect because low dietary calcium can increase oxalate absorption and stone risk. Option B is incorrect because antibiotics do not correct metabolic calcium stone risk. Option C is incorrect because cytology evaluates urothelial malignancy rather than stone chemistry. Option E is incorrect because thiol drugs are for cystinuria, not thiazide-associated hypocitraturia. Teaching point: Thiazides can reduce urinary calcium, but follow-up urine chemistry should guide potassium and citrate management rather than ending prevention planning. Source: American Urological Association. Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline.

compact_payload.source_guideline: Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline
compact_payload.question: A 58-year-old man after total colectomy has recurrent stones, low urine volume, low urinary citrate, and persistently acidic urine. Which prevention plan best addresses the dominant abnormalities?
compact_payload.option_a: Restrict dietary calcium to very low levels
compact_payload.option_b: Increase fluid intake and use potassium citrate
compact_payload.option_c: Start thiol therapy for cystine binding
compact_payload.explanation: Option B is correct. After total colectomy, low urine volume, low urinary citrate, and persistently acidic urine reflect a bowel-loss metabolic phenotype that increases both calcium oxalate and uric acid stone risk. Increased fluid intake to raise urine volume and potassium citrate to alkalinize urine and replenish citrate are the primary interventions. Option A is incorrect because calcium restriction worsens oxalate absorption in malabsorptive states. Option C is incorrect because thiol therapy targets cystinuria. Option D is incorrect because cystoscopy does not prevent metabolic stones. Option E is incorrect because antibiotics do not correct volume, citrate, or pH. Teaching point: Post-colectomy stone phenotype is driven by volume depletion and enteric alkali loss; treatment targets the 24-hour urine abnormalities directly. Source: American Urological Association. Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline.

compact_payload.source_guideline: The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder
compact_payload.question: A 69-year-old woman with idiopathic OAB develops weak stream and recurrent UTIs after intradetrusor botulinum toxin. PVR is now 310 mL. What management issue should be addressed first?
compact_payload.explanation: Option C is correct. After intradetrusor botulinum toxin, new voiding symptoms, recurrent UTIs, and a high PVR should prompt management of incomplete emptying and counseling about retention risk, including catheterization when clinically needed. Option A is incorrect because dose escalation can worsen retention. Option B is incorrect because BCG treats selected NMIBC, not OAB retention. Option D is incorrect because cytology does not treat incomplete emptying. Option E is incorrect because PVR matters when symptoms or UTIs suggest retention. Teaching point: Botulinum toxin can improve urgency while creating a separate safety problem; post-treatment voiding symptoms require PVR-directed management. Source: American Urological Association. The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder.

compact_payload.source_guideline: The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder
compact_payload.question: A 71-year-old woman with severe idiopathic OAB remains profoundly impaired after behavioral therapy, oral medications, neuromodulation, tibial nerve stimulation, and botulinum toxin. What option may be discussed at this refractory stage?
compact_payload.explanation: Option D is correct. In carefully selected patients with severe, refractory OAB who have failed less invasive therapies, augmentation cystoplasty or urinary diversion may be discussed after shared decision-making about morbidity. Option A is incorrect because cytology does not treat OAB. Option B is incorrect because antibiotics do not treat idiopathic urgency without infection. Option C is incorrect because dipstick testing cannot manage end-stage symptoms. Option E is incorrect because BCG treats selected bladder cancer, not idiopathic OAB. Teaching point: Major reconstructive options sit at the far end of the OAB pathway and require failure of conservative, pharmacologic, and minimally invasive choices. Source: American Urological Association. The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder.

compact_payload.question: A 76-year-old man on apixaban has persistent microscopic hematuria confirmed on microscopy. There is no infection, menstruation, or recent instrumentation. How should anticoagulation affect evaluation?
compact_payload.option_a: Stop evaluation because anticoagulation explains it
compact_payload.option_d: Order bone scan as the first test
compact_payload.option_e: Perform the same risk-based hematuria evaluation
compact_payload.explanation: Option E is correct. Patients taking antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy should undergo the same risk-based microhematuria evaluation as patients not taking these agents. Option A is incorrect because anticoagulation can unmask bleeding from malignancy or other pathology. Option B is incorrect because dipstick alone does not complete evaluation of confirmed microhematuria. Option C is incorrect without evidence of infection. Option D is incorrect because bone scan does not evaluate the urinary tract. Teaching point: Do not attribute persistent microhematuria to anticoagulation without applying the usual risk-based urologic algorithm. Source: American Urological Association. Microhematuria: AUA/SUFU Guideline.

compact_payload.source_guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Male Chronic Pelvic Pain: AUA Guideline
compact_payload.question: A 46-year-old man with CP/CPPS has pelvic pain plus erectile dysfunction. Cultures are negative, pelvic floor tenderness is absent, and he wants a medication that may address both domains. What option is reasonable?
compact_payload.explanation: Option C is correct. Daily tadalafil may be prescribed for CP/CPPS patients, including those with concomitant erectile dysfunction, as part of phenotype-directed management. Option A is incorrect because negative cultures argue against chronic antibiotic suppression. Option B is incorrect because ADT treats selected prostate cancer contexts and can worsen sexual function. Option D is incorrect because BCG treats selected NMIBC, not pelvic pain. Option E is incorrect because prostatectomy is not treatment for CP/CPPS. Teaching point: Male chronic pelvic pain management should match the phenotype; sexual dysfunction can make a PDE5 inhibitor a rational component of multimodal care. Source: American Urological Association. Diagnosis and Management of Male Chronic Pelvic Pain: AUA Guideline.

compact_payload.source_guideline: Recurrent Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infections in Women: AUA/CUA/SUFU Guideline
compact_payload.question: A 38-year-old woman with recurrent uncomplicated cystitis has dysuria and frequency. She is stable, has no flank pain, and prior cultures show susceptible E coli. Which treatment approach best fits stewardship guidance?
compact_payload.option_a: Use a short-course first-line agent such as nitrofurantoin
compact_payload.option_b: Use fluoroquinolone therapy as the default first choice
compact_payload.option_c: Treat until follow-up cultures are sterile
compact_payload.option_d: Perform cystoscopy before treating this episode
compact_payload.option_e: Withhold antibiotics because recurrence makes symptoms unreliable
compact_payload.explanation: Option A is correct. Symptomatic acute episodes in recurrent uncomplicated UTI should be treated with short-course first-line agents such as nitrofurantoin, TMP-SMX, or fosfomycin when susceptibility and local resistance patterns support them. Option B is incorrect because fluoroquinolones should not be the default when narrower effective agents are available. Option C is incorrect because sterile follow-up cultures are not the endpoint for an uncomplicated symptomatic episode. Option D is incorrect because cystoscopy is not required before each uncomplicated episode. Option E is incorrect because symptomatic recurrence still warrants treatment. Teaching point: Recurrent UTI stewardship means short, culture-aware treatment of symptomatic episodes, not reflex broad-spectrum therapy or culture eradication. Source: American Urological Association. Recurrent Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infections in Women: AUA/CUA/SUFU Guideline.
